rbin 0.3.0

![](/img/rbin-0-3-0.png){fig-alt="rbin hex logo next to the tagline Binning for credit scoring in R, the line 0.3.0, reliable bins for scorecards, the package name rbin and rbin.rsquaredacademy.com" width="100%"}

```{=html}
<style>
.ba-note{font-size:.88rem;color:#57606a;border-left:3px solid #d0d7de;padding-left:.75rem;margin:.5rem 0 1.25rem}
</style>
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(rbin)
stopifnot(packageVersion("rbin") == "0.3.0")
```

rbin bins numeric predictors for scorecards and reports the weight of evidence and information value of every bin.

rbin 0.3.0 keeps every record in a scorecard in a bin you can explain: missing predictors, repeated values, extreme values and missing responses are each handled, and the package tells you what it did. It also brings in the 0.2.2 and 0.2.3 work, which never reached CRAN. If you saved binning results from 0.2.1, refit before you score; the [Behaviour changes](#behaviour-changes) block lists what moves.

## Install from CRAN

```{r}
#| label: install-cran
#| eval: false
install.packages("rbin")
```

You can see a full list of changes in the [release notes](https://rbin.rsquaredacademy.com/news/).

::: {.ba-note}
How we checked: every 0.3.0 number in this post comes from the code shown, run on CRAN rbin 0.3.0. The 0.2.1 figures come from the same scripts run on CRAN 0.2.1; the scripts and transcripts are in this post's `runs/` folder.
:::

`rbin` bins numeric and categorical predictors for credit scoring models: equal-frequency, quantile, equal-length, winsorized and manual cuts, weight-of-evidence and information-value summaries, and dummy variables built from the bins. The examples use `mbank`, the package's bank marketing data; treat `y` as the good/bad outcome you would model.

## Every customer lands in a bin

Where does a customer with no age go? `mbank` records the outcome of a bank's term-deposit campaign for 4,521 customers, with the age of each. The data has no missing values, so four ages are blanked to mimic incomplete records before `age` is binned into four groups:

```{r}
#| label: missing-predictor
d <- mbank[, c("age", "y")]
missing_rows <- c(which(d$y == "0")[c(2, 5, 9)], which(d$y == "1")[4])
d$age[missing_rows] <- NA
bins_age <- rbin_equal_freq(d, y, age, bins = 4)
bins_age
```

The summary has five bins: four intervals cut from the 4,517 customers who have an age (34, 40 and 49), and a final group of 4 rows marked `NA` in both cut columns ([#69](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/69)). The top interval holds 1,103 rows, and the total information value reads 0.04. The plot shows the weight of evidence for each bin, with the group of rows without an age at the end:

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-bin
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-alt: "Weight of evidence by age bin for 4,521 bank customers, with the four rows without an age as a separate fifth point: -0.14 for up to 34, 0.20 for 34 to 40, 0.27 for 40 to 49, -0.21 for 49 and over, and -0.95 for the rows with no age."
plot(bins_age)
```

In 0.2.1 those four rows sat inside the top interval, whose upper cut printed `NA`; the cuts were 33, 39 and 48, and the total information value read 0.06.

## Bins that match your data

Can a predictor with mostly one value fill five bins? Most customers in `mbank` had no earlier contact: `previous` is zero for 3,686 of them. Ask for five equal-frequency bins:

```{r}
#| label: tied-values
rbin_equal_freq(mbank[, c("previous", "y")], y, previous, bins = 5)
```

Two bins come back, and the message says why. A run of identical values cannot be split across a boundary, so the first bin holds the 3,686 customers with `previous` of 0 and the second holds the rest.

In 0.2.1 the cuts went through the ties: five bins, four of them labelled `0` to `0`, and `rbin_create()` stopped with an error on that summary.

## Score new customers safely

Can a saved set of bins score a customer outside the training range? Credit teams cap a long tail so a handful of extreme values do not set the cuts. Cap `duration` at 100 and 600 seconds and ask for four bins:

```{r}
#| label: winsorize
bins <- rbin_winsorize(
  mbank[, c("duration", "y")], y, duration,
  bins = 4, min_val = 100, max_val = 600
)
bins
```

The cuts are 225, 350 and 475, and the top bin holds 617 customers with a weight of evidence of -1.70. The clamps are stored with the bins, so scoring new records uses the same ones:

```{r}
#| label: score-clamped
rbin_create(data.frame(duration = c(50, 100, 350, 600, 900)), duration, bins)
```

Each value gets one row, with one dummy column marked for the bin it falls in; 50 and 900 fall outside the clamps into the outer bins.

In 0.2.1 the cuts (133.25, 249.5 and 365.75) did not follow the clamps, and the object it saved could not be scored at all: `rbin_create()` stopped on a length mismatch.

rbin takes its cut points from finite predictor values up to 1e300 in absolute value and stops beyond that with a message.

## Clear messages for dropped rows

Where do rows with no outcome go? Three responses are blanked to mimic missing outcomes in this extract:

```{r}
#| label: missing-response
#| warning: true
d <- mbank[, c("age", "y")]
d$y[c(3, 7, 11)] <- NA
rbin_equal_freq(d, y, age, bins = 4)
```

The call drops the three rows, says how many it removed, and summarises the 4,518 that remain: 516 goods, 4,002 bads and an information value of 0.04.

In 0.2.1 the rows stayed in the count and the summary returned `NA` for goods, bads, entropy and information value in every bin that held one, while the count still read 4,521.

## Behaviour changes

If you report bin counts, weight of evidence, information value or dummy variables from bins fitted with 0.2.1, refit before you score.

| What you saved | What moves in 0.3.0 |
|---|---|
| Equal-frequency bins with missing predictors | Missing rows get their own bin, the cuts come from rows with a value, and the top interval count and total information value move (1,130 to 1,103; 0.06 to 0.04 in the `age` example) |
| Bins on tied values | Tied values stay in one bin: ask for 5, get the 2 it can build, and the dummies follow the bins returned |
| Winsorized bins | The clamps bound the fit and the score; a saved 0.2.1 object could not be scored, and `rbin_create()` stopped on a length mismatch |
| Bins with missing responses | Rows without an outcome are dropped with a warning that gives the count, and the summary describes the complete cases |

## Other improvements

- Bare column names, strings and variables that hold names work in every numeric binning function and in `rbin_create()`, including names with spaces or punctuation.
- Character responses are sorted in the same order on every machine, so the second value is always the event; declare the response as a factor to choose the event level yourself.
- Empty intervals keep zero counts and undefined rates and weight of evidence, with zero information value and entropy, instead of dropping out of the summary.
- `rbin_factor()` groups on integer IDs, so two distinct categories whose printed text looks the same stay separate, and an explicit `NA` factor level stays separate from a missing code.
- `rbin_create()` keeps bin order, keeps a column for a bin with no rows, makes colliding boundary labels distinct, and scores values outside the training range into the outer intervals ([#67](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/67)).
- A character predictor is no longer ignored: the numeric methods stop and point to `rbin_factor()` or `rbin_factor_create()` ([#70](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/70)). 64-bit integers (`integer64`) and time differences (`difftime`) are refused with a message showing how to convert them.
- Every method and both addins accept `data.table` input, and a response that is not 0/1, logical or a two-level factor or character stops with a message.
- The package no longer checks CRAN for updates when it is attached.

## What's next

Known issue: a bin with no events or no non-events gets an infinite weight of evidence and information value ([#68](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/68)).

The other open reports concern input checks and messages, not results: argument names in errors and the addins ([#80](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/80)), a one-column matrix predictor ([#79](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/79)), and the conversion hints for date and time predictors ([#77](https://github.com/rsquaredacademy/rbin/issues/77)). The first two are fixed on the development branch and will be in the next release.
